native_result.query: How does age influence the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in?
native_result.HypoA: Younger individuals are more likely to withdraw more money from savings than they had put in and with a negative coefficient between age and withdrawing more than putting into savings (-0.0422).
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. One-hot encode Gender variable into MALE and FEMALE
2. Extract the independent variables ['AGE','INCOME', 'BMI', 'BLACK', 'HISPANIC', 'MALE', 'FEMALE']
3. Add dependent variable (DISSAVED) from the df
4. Add a constant term to the independent variable to account for the intercept term in the logistic regression model.
5. Fit a logistic regression model
native_result.HypoB: Within this young-adult NLSY79 cohort (ages 24-32 only), age is negatively associated with the likelihood of withdrawing more money from savings than putting in (DISSAVED): in the full dataset the predicted probability of dissaving falls from about 25-27% at age 24 to about 19% at age 32 (adjusted logistic model DISSAVED ~ AGE + AGE^2 + controls: AGE coef -0.049 per year, p<0.001, OR~0.95; quadratic term negative, p~0.04, mild inverted-U peaking near age 25), a pattern consistent with weaker present bias / greater patience with age within this narrow window. This association is not robust: it is driven largely by the ~2,200 respondents whose INCOME/BMI are mean-imputed (savings variables default-imputed to 0, skewing older), and after excluding them the age effect is no longer statistically significant and its sign flips slightly positive (P dissaving age 24 vs 32: 0.264 vs 0.286, p>0.1), so the negative age effect should be treated as a feature of the supplied file rather than an established life-course time-preference trend.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/nls_bmi_processed.csv (n=12,686, 0 missing); verified AGE_2==AGE^2, binary outcomes, ranges. 2) Data-quality audit: found 2,151 exact-duplicate rows, traced them to 2,200 rows with mean-imputed INCOME/BMI and default-imputed DISSAVED=0 (older, mean age 29.0); 11 implausible BMI>100 rows dropped from models. 3) Centered AGE at 27.86 to resolve corr(AGE,AGE_2)=0.999 (VIF 687 -> ~1.0). 4) Fit logistic regressions DISSAVED ~ AGE_c + AGE_c2, unadjusted and adjusted for GENDER, log1p(INCOME), BMI, BLACK, HISPANIC, on the full file (primary) and on the non-imputed/deduplicated sample (sensitivity); LR tests for the quadratic term; marginal effects and predicted probabilities at ages 24/28/32. 5) Nonparametric shape check with 3 age bins. 6) Secondary exploratory model for SAMESAVE (separate outcome, perfectly nested with DISSAVED, excluded as covariate). 7) Drafted the data-grounded hypothesis with the duplicate/imputation caveat stated explicitly.

sub_hypo.text: Younger individuals are more likely to withdraw more money from savings than they put in, with an age coefficient of -0.0422.
sub_hypo.context: Respondents in the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY79), with age measured in 1989.
sub_hypo.relations: AGE has a negative coefficient (-0.0422) in a logistic regression predicting DISSAVED, controlling for INCOME, BMI, BLACK, HISPANIC, and gender encoded as MALE and FEMALE. Younger respondents are more likely to have DISSAVED = 1, meaning they withdrew more money from savings than they deposited.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Younger individuals are more likely to withdraw more money from savings than they had put in and with a negative coefficient between age and withdrawing more than putting into savings (-0.0422).

sub_hypo.text: Among NLSY79 respondents aged 24–32 in the supplied full file, age is negatively associated with dissaving after adjustment for gender, income, BMI, and racial background. Predicted dissaving probability falls from about 25–27% at age 24 to about 19% at age 32, with mild inverted-U curvature peaking near age 25. This pattern is consistent with weaker present bias or greater patience within this narrow age window, but does not establish a life-course time-preference trend.
sub_hypo.context: Young-adult NLSY79 cohort aged 24–32; primary analysis of the supplied full file, excluding 11 rows with BMI >100 from models.
sub_hypo.relations: Adjusted logistic association between age and DISSAVED (withdrawing more from savings than depositing): reported age coefficient −0.049 per year, p<0.001, OR approximately 0.95; negative quadratic term, p approximately 0.04, producing mild inverted-U curvature near age 25 and an overall probability decline across ages 24–32. Models center age at 27.86 and adjust for GENDER, log1p(INCOME), BMI, BLACK, and HISPANIC.

sub_hypo.text: The negative age–dissaving association is not robust and is driven largely by approximately 2,200 respondents with mean-imputed income and BMI and default-imputed dissaving values of zero, who skew older. After excluding these respondents in the non-imputed/deduplicated sensitivity sample, the age association becomes slightly positive and statistically nonsignificant, with predicted dissaving probabilities of 0.264 at age 24 and 0.286 at age 32. The negative association should therefore be treated as a feature of the supplied file rather than an established life-course time-preference trend.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 respondents aged 24–32; comparison of the supplied full-file analysis with the non-imputed/deduplicated sensitivity sample. The imputed group has mean age 29.0 and includes 2,151 exact-duplicate rows; models exclude 11 rows with BMI >100.
sub_hypo.relations: The adjusted negative age–DISSAVED association depends on inclusion of older respondents with mean-imputed INCOME/BMI and default-imputed DISSAVED=0. Excluding them reverses the age association slightly and removes statistical significance (p>0.1), with predicted probability increasing from 0.264 at age 24 to 0.286 at age 32.
